title: TB7-14770
frame:
Forum: Refugee Appeal Division (appeal tribunal).
Parties: the appellant and the Minister; names are redacted.
How the layers nest here: The RAD member is the author (layer 1). The appellant and the Minister make submissions to the RAD (layer 2). The RPD decision under appeal is layer 3, and what the claimant or the Minister said to the RPD, as reported, is layer 4.

paragraphs.text: XXXX XXXX (the Appellant) claims that if returned to Turkey, his country of nationality, he will be persecuted based on his political opinion (membership in the HDP (People's Democratic Party)) and his religion (Alevi Muslim). His claim for refugee protection was refused by the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) on July 14, 2017 based on a finding that he lacked credibility and was excluded under Article 1E of the Geneva Convention,1 as he was a permanent resident of Germany. He now appeals to the Refugee Appeal Division (RAD).

Pursuant to paragraph 111(1)(a) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA), I confirm the decision of the RPD that the Appellant is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection. The appeal is dismissed. Factual background

The Appellant claims to be a member of the "Kurdish party (HDP) and Alevi organizations (Pir Sultan Abdal association)." As a result of his political activities, he claims that he was detained, interrogated and tortured by the Turkish authorities. Through the use of an agent/smuggler,2 the Appellant applied for a Canadian visa, which was issued on XXXX XXXX, 2016. In support of the visa application, his agent/smuggler claimed that the Appellant resided in Germany and worked for a German company. A number of documents were submitted, including the Appellant's passport, a German Residency card (said to have been issued by the authorities in XXXX, Germany), banking documents indicating that the Appellant resided in Berlin and a letter from a German company confirming the Appellant's employment. The Appellant arrived in Canada on XXXX XXXX, 2017. He made an inland claim for refugee status on March 27, 2017.

The Appellant has requested the admission of two documents at appeal: i) a letter from the German Consulate in Toronto indicating that the authorities in XXXX "confirmed that there is no registration of a person named XXXX XXXX XXXX, DOB: XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX Citizenship; TURKEY" and ii) an affidavit from a friend of the Appellant, a Mr. XXXX, dated September 25, 2017, outlining the Appellant's political activities in Turkey and in Canada.

Subsection 110(4) of the IRPA limits the admission of evidence in an appeal before the RAD to evidence that: 1) arose after the RPD's rejection of the claim; 2) was not reasonably available at the time of the RPD's rejection of the claim; or 3) an Appellant could not reasonably have been expected in the circumstances to have presented at the time of the RPD's rejection of the claim. RAD rule 3(3)(g)(iii) provides that an Appellant seeking the admission of new evidence must provide full and detailed submissions regarding how the evidence meets the requirements of subsection 110(4) and how that evidence relates to the Appellant. If I find that the new evidence is admissible under subsection 110(4), I must then consider whether the evidence meets the factors elaborated by the Federal Court of Appeal in the Singh case, i.e. newness, credibility and relevance.3 Only then am I able to admit the new evidence. The threshold for the admission of new evidence before the RAD is high.4 i) Letter from the German Consulate

As to the letter from the German Consulate, the Appellant does not offer an explanation as to why he could not have obtained this letter before the RPD's rejection of his claim. An affidavit in support of the request for the admission of the document merely notes that the document was requested on August 4, 2017 and the Appellant's Legal Memorandum states that the "piece of evidence was not present at the time of the hearing before the RPD".5 No argument is made as to why the information from the German Consulate was not sought until after the rejection of the claim. Nor does the Appellant indicate why the document was not reasonably available or could not reasonably have been expected to be presented at the time of the RPD's rejection of the claim.

Normally, my consideration of the matter would end here: it does not fall to me to make an argument for an Appellant where none has been made by him or his counsel. However, in the circumstances, I feel that fairness requires me to look at the background of the issue. The hearing was originally scheduled for May 29, 2017, but was adjourned in order to ensure that the Ministry-which had earlier requested permission from the Appellant to contact the German authorities in relation to a possible Article 1E exclusion-received the signed permission document from the Appellant. The hearing resumed on July 29, 2017; however the Ministry-despite its earlier request-declined to intervene. Because of the Ministry's initial interest in contacting the German authorities, it was reasonable, I find, for the Appellant not to have done so. As such, I find that the Appellant could not reasonably have been expected in the circumstances to have presented the letter from the German consulate at the time of the RPD's rejection of the claim.

I must now turn to the Singh factors, i.e. newness, credibility and relevance. Based on my examination of the document, I can see no basis to find that it is lacking in credibility. It is on letterhead, is signed and appears official. It is clearly new information and it is highly relevant to an essential finding of the RPD: that the Appellant had permanent residency in Germany. Consequently, I find the document admissible. ii) Affidavit from Mr.

Once again, the Appellant offers no argument as to how the affidavit from Mr. XXXX XXXX sworn September 25, 2017, complies with subsection 110(4). It is clear from its content, that it contains no information that could not have been either provided to the RPD at the time of the Appellant's hearing or during the period after the last session of the hearing (June 29, 2017) and before the Appellant's claim was rejected (July 14, 2017). As such, I find it inadmissible. Hearing

The Appellant has also requested that the RAD hold a hearing in relation to the new evidence in the following terms: The Appellant is asking to have hearing [sic] before the RAD pursuant to section 110(6) of the IRPA. The RPD did not address issue credibility [sic] as it solely based its decision on exclusion under Article 1A [sic]. There is also new evidence by of Affidavit from Mr. XXXX. The RAD may wish to hear evidence from Mr. XXXX.6

The principle under subsection 110(3) of the IRPA that the RAD must proceed without a hearing, is subject to an exception, elaborated in subsection 110(6). The latter subsection provides a hearing may be held where three conditions in relation to the new evidence are met. The new evidence must: a) raise a serious issue with respect to the Appellant's credibility; b) be central to the decision with respect to his refugee protection claim and c) if accepted, justify allowing or rejecting his claim.

The Appellant's justification for his request for a hearing centres primarily on the affidavit of Mr. XXXX; given my finding above that his affidavit is inadmissible, I need not have regard to the existence of the three conditions outlined in subsection 110(6) in relation to that affidavit. As to the letter from the German Consulate, I find that the test at section 110(6) is not met: the evidence, though admitted, does not "justify allowing or rejecting his claim." The evidence certainly impacts on the RPD's finding-discussed below-that the Appellant's residence permit in Germany excludes him based on Article 1E; however that alone does not justify allowing or rejecting the Appellant's claim. The issue of his credibility remains.

The determinative issues in this case are i) whether the Appellant is disqualified from refugee protection in Canada under Article 1E of the Geneva Convention by virtue of having been recognized as a resident of Germany and ii) credibility.

The standard of review is correctness,7 except where the RPD enjoys a meaningful advantage in the assessment of the oral testimony. If such an advantage exists, I will apply a standard of reasonableness.8 Where I do so, I will so indicate.

The RPD found, on a balance of probabilities, that the Appellant had permanent residence in Germany. It also found that the Appellant lacked credibly as he had submitted a falsified passport when making his refugee claim. The Appellant argues that he was not a resident of Germany and that the RPD's finding that he lacked credibility was in error. i) German residency and Article 1E

The RPD, noting that the Canadian visa officials had accepted the documents submitted in support of the Appellant's visa application, found that they were, on a balance of probabilities, authentic and found further that he had, as indicated in the visa application, permanent residency in Germany.

The Appellant argues that all of the documents that were a part of his Canadian visa application, other than his passport, were forgeries. He argues that the RPD erred in finding that the Canadian officials who reviewed the visa application would have made a determination that the documentation was genuine; there was no evidence to this effect. Simply because the documentation was realistic enough to fool the visa officials did not mean that it was genuine. He notes that "it is quite likely that, when came [sic] across such documents that are forget [sic] sophisticatedly, the Visa officer may take them as genuine."9

As noted, I have admitted into evidence the letter from the German Consulate indicating that the residency card was not valid and I can see no indication that that letter is anything other than authentic. As such, an important aspect of the RPD's finding that the Appellant had permanent residency in Germany is missing and I must review its finding on this point.

Even though I have no reason to find that the other documents submitted as part of the Appellant's visa application were invalid, because the Residency Card is not valid, I do not share the RPD's conclusion that the Appellant was a German resident. I find, on a balance of probabilities, that the Appellant did not have permanent residency in Germany and that the RPD erred in finding that he was excluded from refugee protection by virtue of Article 1E. ii) Credibility

The RPD reviewed the Appellant's passport and found that there were two versions. In the version that was submitted to the Canadian officials in late 2016 in support of the Appellant's visa application, all pages appeared to be from the same passport and there was evidence of extensive travel on the part of the Appellant. In the second version, the one submitted as part of the Appellant's refugee claim in late March 2017, certain of the passport's pages-in particular the pages that, in the version submitted to the Canadian visa officials, featured stamps showing extensive travel-featured numbers that indicated that they were from a different passport.

The RPD suggested that the most likely explanation for the existence of two versions of the passport was that the Appellant's real passport was used in the application for a Canadian visa but that after the passport had been returned to the Appellant (with the Canadian visa in it), it had been modified in such a way that the Appellant's connections with Germany would be hidden, so they would not undermine his Canadian refugee claim. When confronted with this, the Appellant denied all knowledge attributed any fraud to his agent/smuggler:10 RPD: Okay. Sir if you take a look more closely at the two pages, the numbers on the top of the pages are different. Why would the numbers be different? Appellant: The smugglers play with the passport pages. RPD: Okay. So in examining those pages I'll show you what I found. So we have established that the photo pages that I showed you between the [Canadian visa] application and [the version of the passport submitted in support of the refugee claim] are the same. The passport number on both of those on the photo page is as follows: XXXX. Now the visa pages 6 to 9 for the [Canadian visa application] copy, that is the one with the stamps, I can read the numbers on top of that. They also read XXXX, so those numbers are the same as they should be. The visa pages in the [version of the passport submitted in support of the refugee claim] have a different number at the top they say XXXX. So not only does that the visa pages match the number in the other passport it is not even the same numbers what is in the same photo page that is supposed to be in the same document. Can you explain that? Appellant: I have no reasonable explanation to that Mr. Member and I have no idea what was done because I obtained my passport through the regular passport office and I provide to the smugglers. I have no idea what they have done with the passport. The RPD rejected this explanation. As discussed above, it noted that that the Canadian officials would have examined the passport as part of the visa application process; had it been tampered with at the time of their examination, the officials would not have issued the visa.

The Appellant claims that he provided a valid passport to the agent/smuggler.11 However, at the same time, he claims that he had never travelled outside Turkey until he came to Canada. Given that the version of the passport that was submitted to the Canadian visa officials featured a number of stamps showing extensive travel on his part, the only way those two statements could be reconciled would be if the passport submitted to the Canadian visa officials was valid but the stamps were forged. As noted above, the Appellant argues that the RPD erred in finding that the Canadian official who reviewed the visa application would have made a determination that the documentation was genuine; simply because the documentation was realistic enough to fool the visa official, did not mean that it was genuine.

I have closely examined the two versions of the Appellant's passport-the version that was submitted to Canadian visa officials and one that was submitted to as part of the Appellant's refugee claim-and confirm that the RPD was correct in finding that they were different. With both versions the passport number is given on the front cover and on the photograph page (page 2) as XXXX. While the version of the passport that was submitted as part of the application for the Canadian visa has the same passport number, XXXX, stamped on all of the pages provided, the version that was submitted as part of the Appellant's refugee claim does not. In the latter version of the passport, pages 1 (the cover) - 3 show the number XXXX; however, on pages 4 - 12 the passport number stamped on the document pages is XXXX. At page 13 the passport number returns to XXXX. The numbers on most other pages are not entirely legible, however it is clear that pages 22 and 23 are stamped with a passport number ending in "XXXX"-presumably XXXX-and pages 52 and 53 are stamped with a number ending in "XXXX"-presumably XXXX. The Canadian visa, found at page 20, is linked to passport number XXXX; the passport number stamped on that page is not legible.

I find, on a balance of probabilities, that the passport submitted to the Canadian visa officials was authentic. Had the clumsily modified version been submitted to the visa officials, they would, on a balance of probabilities, have noticed. After all, their role is to ensure that applications for visas are legitimate.

It is clear that the version submitted in support of the Appellant's refugee claim had substituted pages that corresponded with those pages in the passport submitted as part of the visa application where there was evidence of travel (pages 6 - 12).12 Consequently, I find, on a balance of probabilities, that there was an attempt to fraudulently modify the passport so that the travel stamps would not appear in the modified version.

The question then becomes when the pages were removed and why. As noted, it is the position of the Appellant that he gave the agent/smuggler his valid passport and that any substitution of pages was the work of the agent/smuggler. In order for this argument to hold water, the agent/smuggler would have not only had to modify the passport with sufficient sophistication to fool Canadian visa officials, he would have also had to replace the pages containing the stamps after it was returned to the agent/smuggler from the Canadian visa officials but before the agent/smuggler returned it to the Appellant. Such a scenario would mean that the Appellant would have entered Canada on a passport that featured pages stamped as being from two different passports. This is not only implausible-given that Canadian Border Security Agency (CBSA) officials are charged with ensuring that people entering Canada do so lawfully-it is also illogical: there would be no advantage to the agent/smuggler modifying the passport before the Appellant travelled and considerable disadvantage. After all, the Appellant would be presenting himself to Canadian border officials with a rather obviously altered passport.

I am of the view that it is implausible that a passport, doctored in the rather clumsy way described, would not have been spotted by the CBSA officials if it had been was presented at Pearson Airport on XXXX XXXX, 2017. Consequently, I find on a balance of probabilities, that the Appellant travelled to Canada on his unaltered passport.

The foregoing leaves me to conclude that, on a balance of probabilities, the passport was tampered with by the Appellant (or under his direction) sometime after the Appellant's arrival in Canada and before he surrendered it as part of his refugee claim. While the Appellant's motives for modifying his passport are unknowable, he may have thought that removing evidence of foreign travel would strengthen his refugee claim-perhaps by eliminating any risk that he would be faulted for not having made a claim in one of the countries to which he had travelled. I find that this act of fraud seriously undermines the Appellant's credibility.

I find, on a balance of probabilities, that the travel stamps-which show extensive travel, including to Germany-are valid and that his testimony that he had never set foot outside Germany until he came to Canada was a fabrication. I find that this fabrication seriously undermines his credibility. Conclusion regarding credibility

As noted, I have found that the Appellant has fraudulently altered his passport and that his testimony that he had never left Turkey was fabricated. However, before making a final finding regarding the Appellant's credibility, I turn to the supporting documents provided to the RPD. In addition to the fraudulently altered passport, the Appellant has submitted a Turkish identity card showing him to have the same name and date of birth as the person in each version of the passport.13 The only other documents provided by the Appellant are receipts for the payment of membership fees to the HDP, receipts for the payment of membership fees to the Pir Sultan Abdal Cultural Association, a membership card from the Pir Sultan Abdal Cultural Association, a letter from the Canadian Alevi Culture Centre and photographs said to be of the Appellant. I will consider each in turn.

The receipts for payment of membership fees to the HDP appear valid on their face and pertain to two years during which the Appellant claims to have been a party member. I find they have probative value and support the Appellant's assertion that he was a member of the HDP.
The payments for membership fees and the membership card in the Pir Sultan Abdal Cultural Association appear valid, have probative value and support the Appellant's claim that he was an Alevi Muslim.

The letter from the Canadian Alevi Culture Centre, dated April 16, 2017, states that the Appellant is a member of the Alevi faith and had been a member of the community centre since March 2017. I note that the letter does not make clear how the Centre arrived at its finding that he was a member of the Alevi faith. Nevertheless, I assign the letter some probative value.

Finally, the Appellant submitted six photographs said to be pictures of him.14 I have reviewed the photographs and can see no indication that the Appellant features in any of them. The first three pictures said to be taken at protests in Turkey; however, they feature multiple people (as many as 40), none of whom appears to be the Appellant. I assign these no probative value. The other three photographs are said to be taken at a time when the Appellant was here in Canada. Even accepting that these are pictures of the Appellant, they are of limited probative value. The fact that he has participated in Kurdish political events while in Canada does not prove that he did so in Turkey. He may well have participated in the events in Canada with a view to strengthening a false refugee claim.

When I weigh the Appellant's fraudulent behaviour, as outlined above, against to the documents outlined above and their probative value, I find that the Appellant is, overall, lacking in credibility. Consequently, I find that his claims of persecution by the Turkish state on the basis of his membership in the HDP are, on a balance of probabilities, false. Forward facing fear as an Alevi Muslim

Even given my finding that the Appellant lacked credibility-and, as such, that his evidence that he active in the HDP is not to be believed-it falls to me to consider whether someone similarly situated as a Alevi Muslim in Turkey would face a serious possibility of persecution or would face, on a balance of probabilities, harm of the nature outlined in subsection 97(1) of the IRPA.

I have reviewed documents submitted by the Appellant before the RPD, only two of which touch on the situation of Alevi Muslims in Turkey,15 as well as the National Documentation Package. The two articles submitted by the Appellant before the RPD are of limited value: the first deals with an incident from 1993 and is not relevant to the situation in 201816 and the second makes only passing reference to a single incident involving an attack against Alevi neighbourhoods during the attempted coup in 2016.17

It is clear from the objective evidence that the 15 - 20 million Alevi Muslims in Turkey18 face inequalities. These include not having their places of worship officially recognized (and, therefore, not receiving financial support from the state),19 difficulties establishing new places of worship,20 a refusal to allow Alevi children an exemption from compulsory Sunni Islamic instruction;21 and an inability to state their religion on their identify cards (the government considers Alevism a heterodox Muslim sect).22 There have also been a small number of reports of ill-treatment of Alevis by the authorities,23 primarily in the context of demonstrations by the Alevi community.24 Isolated incidents of societal discrimination and violence towards Alevis have been reported but "these are few and most Alevis co-exist with other communities with few problems on a daily basis."25

The UK Home Office offers the following summary: Even when taken cumulatively, the treatment faced by Alevis does not in general amount to them being subject to action on the part of either non-state actors or the authorities which would amount to persecution or serious harm.26 I agree with this summary. I find that, despite the existence of problems, Alevi Muslims in general do not face a serious possibility of persecution in Turkey.

Based the foregoing, I find the Appellant will not face a serious possibility of persecution on his return to Turkey. I find further that, on a balance of probabilities, he will not face harm of the nature described in subsection 97(1) of the IRPA.

The Appeal is dismissed.
